analysis.one_liner: Authorizes sanctions on foreign spyware companies that help target U.S. officials.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in September 2023 and never received a hearing, vote, or cosponsor before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let the President freeze the U.S. assets and revoke the U.S. visas of foreign companies and individuals who sell or use commercial spyware that has been used to target U.S. government officials or intelligence personnel. It aims to deter foreign governments from buying phone-hacking tools used to spy on officials, silence dissidents, and track Americans. It sat in committee with no cosponsors and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. government officials, intelligence personnel, and by extension ordinary Americans whose phones could be targeted by foreign-purchased hacking tools; also dissidents and journalists abroad whom authoritarian governments target with spyware.
analysis.who_benefits_short: U.S. officials, journalists, and phone users

how_it_helps.text: Lets the President block the U.S. property and transactions of foreign companies and individuals who sell or use spyware that has enabled targeting of U.S. government officials or intelligence personnel [S3].
Makes such sanctioned foreign persons inadmissible to the United States and automatically revokes any existing U.S. visas, cutting them off from the American financial and travel system [S3].
States a U.S. policy of deterring spyware used to intimidate opponents, curb dissent, limit free expression and assembly, and enable human rights abuses [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Foreign commercial spyware companies, their executives, and the foreign governments that buy their tools, who would face asset freezes and visa bans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Foreign spyware firms and their executives

drawbacks.text: The sanctions are discretionary and cover only spyware that has targeted U.S. government officials or intelligence personnel — not spyware sold to spy on ordinary citizens, journalists, or dissidents abroad, which is the more common use [S3].
The bill explicitly carves out U.S. intelligence and law enforcement activities and bars the President from banning imports of the sanctioned firms' goods, leaving significant loopholes [S3].
Enforcement depends entirely on a President's willingness to designate companies, and the authority expires after 7 years, so it provides no guaranteed protection [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A modest, targeted tool against a real national-security and privacy threat, but narrow: it only reaches spyware used against U.S. officials, exempts U.S. intelligence activity, and relies entirely on discretionary presidential designations.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Foreign Affairs and Judiciary committees in September 2023 and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. James Himes introduced the bill on September 18, 2023 [S1].
It was referred to the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
No action was taken after referral: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill attracted zero cosponsors [S4].
All bills pending at the end of a Congress expire and must be reintroduced to move again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign commercial spyware companies: no new U.S. sanctions, asset freezes, or visa bans were enacted, and the status quo continues.

for.name: Rep. James A. Himes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Foreign Affairs and Judiciary committees; the bill gained no cosponsors during the Congress.

against.name: House Foreign Affairs Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor vote was ever held, and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: These firms sell phone-hacking tools to governments that use them to target officials, journalists, and dissidents; the bill would cut them off from the U.S. financial system and travel. Because the bill died, they faced no new restrictions.
U.S. companies and government intelligence activity are explicitly exempted, so domestic surveillance-adjacent firms lose nothing; the bill only reaches foreign firms.
